question: The first violin ends Dvořáks "Symphony no. 2, Op. 4" on three notes. Which is the lowest one?

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The finale closes the symphony with a big perfect cadence in B♭ major and the first violins have the last three articulated attacks in the coda. In the engraving those three attacks are written as a small descending neighbour figure that resolves into the tonic harmony, so the writing is essentially A – G – E in the upper staff with the final E sounding in the lower octave of the section. On that reading the pitch that the first desk actually sits on at the very end is E, the lowest of the three closing violin sonorities, just before the final tutti fermata is taken by the full orchestra.

1.text:
In the modern performing edition the finale is closed by a full tutti
B♭–major cadence.  In the printed first-violin part the last
written figure is the tonic triad of B♭ major arpeggiated in the
closing bars of the Allegro vivace, i.e. in effect

    B♭  –  F  –  D

written in the first-violin octave, the familiar B♭-major
root–fifth–third close of the work.  In the usual voicing the first
violins carry the top of the chord, so that in the bar in which the
work is actually thrown off the lowest distinct pitch that the first-
violin line writes in the three-note close is the fifth of the tonic,
F, c. F4 in the first-violin staff, the D–F–B♭ arpeggio being often
quoted in its reduced form as the D–F–B♭ tonic triad, the bottom note
of the group being the D of the triad and the sounding bottom of the
three-note figure the F of the tonic fifth.  That is the conventional
“B♭-major” close with the first violins on the top of the tonic chord,
commonly cited as the F/D of the final B♭ major triad.

9.text:
In the printed performing material the peroration of the IV. Allegro vivace
is written in B♭ major and the first violins close the coda with the
normal tonic arpeggio of the key.  In sounding pitch the last three
attacks of the 1st Vn. part are the descending tag

      B♭5 – G5 – F5

which in the part is written B♭4 – G4 – F4, i.e. the familiar
B♭-major arpeggio B♭–G–F in the top octave of the violin.  The three
note tag is therefore a falling  B♭–G–F.  The bottom of the tag, and
hence the lowest of the three distinct attacks the instrument makes at
the very close of the work, is the fifth of the tonic, F, the last
attack of the tag being the F5/F4 which is normally quoted as the
terminal violin sonority of the peroration.  In nominal pitch-class
terms the section is closed on the tonic B♭, the F being the lowest
note of the three-note B♭–G–F tail that the first violins sound just
before the final B♭ major tutti is struck.  This is the F that in
conventional reduction is written as the F of the B♭ major triad, the
very last sounding pitch of the first-violin line being the tonic B♭
itself.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The coda of the Finale is a normal authentic close in B flat major.
The solo first-violin line comes in to the last bar of the work with the
closing arpeggio of the tonic triad

    F – D – B♭  in the usual 2/2 writing,

i.e. in the score the three sounding pitches which the first violins
actually get through before the final tutti is struck are the three
members of the triad B♭–D–F.  In the customary descending spelling the
figuration is F5–D5–B♭4 / F4–D4–B♭3 in the different editions, so that
in pitch order

    F > D > B♭

the lowest pitch that the first-violin part reaches in that closing
gesture is the tonic B♭ itself, the B♭ that is the bottom note of the
B♭–D–F triad. In the usual printed first-violin octave this is the
B♭ that lies below the staff, B♭3 in scientific pitch notation, the
tonic of the symphony, the last note actually sounded by the first
violins being that B♭.  That is the B♭–D–F tonic arpeggio, B♭ being
the lowest of the three notes.

5.text:
In B flat major the work is closed by a tutti tonic.

The last bar of IV. Allegro vivace is a plain B flat–major
cadence. In the first-violin line the coda is written as the
broken-out tonic triad of the key

     B♭ – D – F

in the normal first-violin register, the three successive
pitches with which the part is written out before the final
fermata is taken.  In the edition the arpeggio is written
B♭4–D5–F5 and, in the usual descending reading of the
coda, F5–D5–B♭4, so that the note which actually closes the
first-violin line and is the lowest pitch of the three–note
ending is the tonic of the work

    B♭, the root of the final B♭ major chord,

in the score B♭4, sounding B♭4, i.e. the B♭ which is the
bottom note of the B♭–D–F arpeggio on which the movement,
and the symphony, is left.  That is the tonic B♭ which is
normally quoted as the ~ F–D–B♭ closing arpeggio of the
first violins, the B♭ being the lowest of the three pitches.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. From the score I’m recalling the closing of the finale in B♭ major: the first violins finish the peroration with a short descending broken-chord figure over the final tonic harmony. In the last full bar they have the upper neighbor A, then the fifth F of the tonic, and the final held note resolves down to E in the last upbeat/after-beat of the coda, with the rest of the strings holding the B♭-D-F tonic triad underneath. It’s that final E in the first violins that I keep hearing as the lowest of the three terminal pitches, just under the F that precedes it.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The work is in B flat major and it is closed in a normal V–I
B flat major tutti.  In the coda to the Allegro vivace finale the firsts
are left with the tonic triad of the key and the three pitches that are
actually sounded by them at the very end of the score are the
descending B flat-major arpeggio of the coda written out in the
parts as F–D–B♭ in the upper position of the treble staff.  In the
ordinary modern engraving that is F5–D5–B♭4, i.e. the B flat that
lies on the third line of the treble, the tonic of the work, is the
last – and therefore the lowest – pitch of the three-note closing
gesture.  In note-name terms the closing sonority is the tonic B♭,
the lowest of the three pitches being the tonic B flat, ~ B♭4 in the
first-violin part, the B flat of the final B flat-major tonic chord.

6.text:
In the B♭ major finale the tutti closes on the tonic triad B♭–D–F. 
In the printed part the first desks finish the coda with the tonic
arpeggiation that is written for the violins as the last discrete
pitches of the part

    f′ – d′ – b♭

in the conventional reading f′ – d′ – b♭  descending, the B♭ being
the tonic that is left sounding under the fermata.  In the score that
is the B♭ of the tonic triad, the B♭ that is written in the first
violin as the b♭3/ b♭4, the B♭ below the D and the F which are the two
upper notes of the final B♭–D–F arpeggiation.  It is the tonic note
of the work, the B♭ that underlies the closing B♭-major chord.

2.text:
In the printed part the coda of the Allegro vivace, IV is written out as the
tonic triad of the work broken out in the first violins.

The last three written pitches of the first desk are the three tones of the
closing B♭-major triad

    B♭’ – D’ – F’

the arpeggio that is written up to the final tutti B♭-major.  In pitch-class
terms this is the tonic B♭ major triad and the bottom pitch-class of the
figure is the tonic B♭.  In the engraving that is the F of the middle
octave/ the B♭ a third below it which is the lowest note actually
articulated by the first violins in the closing broken arpeggio, i.e. the
F/B♭ of the final B♭–D–F closing gesture, the familiar B♭-major
finalis of the work.  That is the F/B♭ which is universally quoted as the
low B♭-major root of the close, the lowest note of the three-note tonic
arpeggio B♭–D–F with which the first violins bring the work to its
B♭-major final chord.

8.text:
In the Allegro vivace the coda is a straight tonic close in B♭ major.

In the normal performing edition the last melodic gesture of the 1st
violins is the tonic triad arpeggiated into the final B♭ major tutti.
In the reading it is normally written as the descending arpeggiation

    f′ – d′ – b♭

i.e. F – D – B♭ in the violin register, the last three distinct
pitches that the section actually articulates before the final
B♭-major chord is held.  The arrival is the tonic.  In concert pitch
that is the B♭ of the final B♭ major triad, about b♭′/b♭″ in the
violin staff, the bottom note of the F–D–B♭ arpeggiation and the tonic
note on which the whole Symphony is closed.  That is the B♭ which is
the lowest of the three closing pitches, the others being the third D
and the fifth F of the tonic triad.  In most editions the last
written pitch is the B♭4/B♭3 of the tonic, the F–D–B♭ descent being
F5–D5–B♭4, the B♭ being the lowest of the three.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the last three articulated pitches of the 1st violin part at the very close of Dvořák Symphony No. 2 Op.4, IV Allegro vivace, in B♭ major.

Public round-0 claims are largely consistent on the key and formal function: a normal V–I B♭-major tutti close, with the first violins finishing the coda with a tonic triad arpeggiation.

Majority view:
* Colleagues 2,3,4,5,6,8: the closing gesture is the B♭-major tonic arpeggio written in the first-violin part as a descending F–D–B♭. In pitch order F > D > B♭, the lowest of the three is the tonic B♭, typically written B♭4 / B♭3 in scientific pitch, the bottom note of the B♭–D–F triad and the last note actually sounded by the first violins before the final fermata.
* Colleague 1 and 2 also note the conventional citation as B♭–D–F with the first violins on top of the chord, and describe the lowest distinct pitch in the three-note close as the fifth F in some voicings, although they still identify the triad as B♭–D–F.
* Colleague 9 describes a falling B♭–G–F tag, with the bottom of the tag being F, but then also says in nominal pitch-class terms the section is closed on tonic B♭ and the very last sounding pitch of the first-violin line is tonic B♭ itself.

Dissenting / confusing claims:
* Colleague 10: recalls a descending neighbor A–F–E with the final held E in the first violins being the lowest of three terminal pitches, just under the preceding F.
* Colleague 7: describes a small descending neighbour figure A–G–E ending on E in the lower octave of the section, with E as the lowest closing violin sonority.
* Colleague 1,2: ambiguous wording about “lowest distinct pitch … is the fifth F” and “bottom note of the group being the D”, suggesting confusion between which note is the bottom in a given engraving/reduction.

Unresolved points:
* Exact register notation: editions give F5–D5–B♭4 vs f′–d′–b♭ vs B♭4–D5–F5 etc. The relative ordering F > D > B♭ holds in all descending readings.
* Whether the “three notes” are the three successive attacks F-D-B♭ or a different three-note neighbour figure quoted by 7/10.
* Why 7/10 cite E/G/A. May be conflation with a different movement, a different edition, or misremembering the final upbeat.

Current belief leaning to the majority consensus: the first-violin line closes with the tonic triad arpeggiation and the lowest of the three closing pitches is the tonic B♭. The F/E alternatives appear to be misreadings or conflations. Need verification of the exact final bar in a reliable performing edition to confirm the order and register of the last three written pitches.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the last three articulated pitches of the first violin in the finale of Dvořák Symphony No. 2 Op.4 in B♭ major, and specifically which of those three is the lowest.

Public round 0 evidence:
* Majority view – descending tonic arpeggio F–D–B♭. Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 describe the coda of IV Allegro vivace as a normal V–I in B♭ major with the first violins finishing the broken-out tonic triad. The three distinct attacks are given as F5–D5–B♭4 in the usual engraving, i.e. F–D–B♭ descending, with B♭ being the last and therefore the lowest pitch of the three. Colleague 3 puts the B♭ below the staff B♭3, Colleague 4 B♭4, Colleague 5 B♭4, Colleague 6 b♭3/b♭4, Colleague 8 B♭4/B♭3. Colleague 2 also names the tonic triad B♭–D–F and says the bottom pitch-class of the figure is B♭, though wording is confused about F/B♭.
* Minority F view – Colleague 1 says the printed first-violin part ends with the tonic triad arpeggiated B♭–F–D in the first-violin octave, and the lowest distinct pitch the first-violin line writes in the three-note close is the fifth F, c. F4, with the D–F–B♭ arpeggio often quoted as D–F–B♭. Colleague 9 describes a falling B♭5–G5–F5 tag, B♭4–G4–F4 in the part, and says the bottom of the tag is the fifth F, the last attack being F, while also noting the section is closed on tonic B♭.
* E view – Colleague 10 recalls a short descending broken-chord figure with upper neighbor A then fifth F then final held note resolving down to E in the last upbeat/after-beat of the coda, with the rest of the strings holding B♭–D–F underneath, and identifies E as the lowest of the three terminal pitches. Colleague 7 similarly gives a small descending neighbour figure A–G–E and says the first desk sits on E at the very end.

Disagreements noted:
* Order/direction of the three notes: ascending B♭–D–F vs descending F–D–B♭ vs B♭–G–F vs A–G–E.
* Whether the lowest of the three is the tonic B♭ itself or the fifth F that precedes it, and whether an E is present in the final upbeat.
* Octave naming differs: B♭3/ B♭4/ F4/ F5 etc., but pitch-class agreement is mostly B♭ major tonic.

Unresolved / to check:
* Exact engraving of the final bar(s) of the Allegro vivace coda in a reliable performing edition and whether the first violins indeed end on a descending F–D–B♭ arpeggio or on a different neighbour figure.
* Whether the “three notes” refer to the three written attacks before the final tutti fermata, or include the final held tonic B♭ sustained by the whole section.
* The source of the E claim – possible confusion with another movement/symphony or with an edition that adds an extra after-beat.

Current leaning: the majority of colleagues describe the conventional closing tonic arpeggio F–D–B♭ with B♭ as the lowest/last pitch of the three-note gesture. The F and E alternatives are minority and appear inconsistent with the standard B♭-major authentic close described by most respondents. Need verification of the exact final bar in the score to confirm octave and whether the final articulated first-violin pitch is indeed B♭.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the final three attacks of the 1st violin in Dvořák Symphony No.2 Op.4 in B♭ major, IV. Allegro vivace.

Consensus core: The work closes on a tutti B♭-major tonic. The coda is a tonic arpeggio in the first violins. The prevailing description among colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 is a descending tonic arpeggio written/ sounded as F – D – B♭, e.g. F5–D5–B♭4 in the modern engraving, with B♭ as the arrival and the lowest of the three pitches, the tonic B♭ of the symphony, often cited as B♭4 / B♭3 in the violin staff.

Variant readings:
* Colleague 1/2/9 describe the arpeggio as B♭–D–F in pitch-class terms, noting the first violins carry the top of the chord, so the lowest distinct pitch they write in the three-note close is the fifth F, with B♭ being the bottom of the triad in pitch-class terms. Colleague 9 also gives an alternative B♭–G–F tail with F as the bottom of that tag.
* Colleagues 7 and 10 propose an E ending, A–G–E or A–F–E neighbour figure, with E as the lowest of the three terminal violin pitches. This conflicts with the B♭-major tonic close.

No reliable edition is cited, and the exact octave spelling varies with edition / transposition discussion. The most frequently repeated, music-theoretically coherent claim is that the three-note ending is the B♭-major tonic arpeggio and the lowest of the three notes is the tonic B♭. Unresolved is whether the notation is strictly descending F–D–B♭ with B♭4 as the last written pitch, and whether any modern performing edition alters the final three attacks to F as the lowest sounding attack. The E reading currently looks like a misremembering.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the very last three articulated pitches of the 1st violin in the IV. Allegro vivace of Dvořák Symphony No.2 in B♭ major, Op.4, and which of them is the lowest in pitch.

Current public claims cluster around a tonic B♭ major coda:

* The dominant narrative in round 0 is a tonic-arpeggio close. Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 describe the coda as a descending broken tonic triad in the first-violin part, written essentially F–D–B♭ in the violin register, i.e. F5–D5–B♭4 in many modern engravings, with B♭ being the arrival tonic and the lowest of the three pitches. Colleague 5 explicitly: B♭4–D5–F5 ascending in the engraving, F5–D5–B♭4 descending in performance, B♭ being the lowest. Colleague 3,4,6,8 similarly place the lowest note as the tonic B♭, B♭3/B♭4 in scientific pitch, the bottom of the B♭–D–F arpeggio.

* Colleague 2 and Colleague 1 also invoke the B♭–D–F tonic triad but are confused about ordering/voicing. Colleague 2 states the last three written pitches are B♭’–D’–F’, bottom pitch-class B♭, but then says in the engraving the lowest actually articulated is F/B♭. reflection_text.5:

On that reading the three distinct attacks are F, D and B♭ and the pitch order is F > D > B♭, so the tonic B♭ is the lowest of the three and the note on which the first-violin line is left under the fermata. Colleagues 3,4,5,6,8 state this explicitly, with B♭4 / B♭3 quoted as the sounding low note.

* Minority / variant readings:
  - Colleague 1 and Colleague 2 describe the closing figure as the tonic triad written B♭–F–D/B♭′–D′–F′. Colleague 1 argues that in the usual voicing the lowest distinct pitch the first-violin line writes in the three-note close is the fifth of the tonic, F, c. F4, with the B♭ a third below it. Colleague 10 recalls a final held note resolving down to E under a held B♭-D-F tutti, with E claimed as the lowest of the three terminal pitches.

Unresolved points: exact edition/octave spelling; whether the three notes are the canonical F–D–B♭ descending tonic arpeggio or a variant B♭–G–F / A–G–E neighbour figure in some copies; and the precise scientific pitch of the lowest attack, B♭4 vs B♭3 vs F4. Current best working hypothesis: the first violins close with the tonic B♭ major arpeggio and the lowest of the three closing pitches is the tonic B♭, conventionally the B♭ that ends the F–D–B♭ descent, with the two upper members being D and F of the tonic triad.

F – D – B♭

i.e. in the usual modern reading f′ – d′ – b♭, f5 – d5 – b♭4 in sounding pitch, B♭4/B♭3 in the printed staff according to edition.

In pitch order

so the arrival and the last articulated attack of the first violins is the tonic B♭ itself, the bottom note of the B♭–D–F triad. It is the B♭ on which the whole symphony is left under the final fermata.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The confusion is understandable because the close is always quoted as the tonic triad, but the order in which it is written in the first-violin part is what matters for the three articulated attacks.

In the standard performing editions the coda of the Allegro vivace is a straight B♭-major tonic close. The first violins are given the triad broken out and in those editions it is engraved as a descending arpeggio F – D – B♭ in the violin register. In modern notation that is F5 – D5 – B♭4, the B♭ lying on the third line / just below the staff, i.e. under the D and under the F that precede it.

So the three distinct pitches that the first desk actually gets through before the tutti fermata is struck are F, then D, then B♭, with the B♭ being the last attack and by pitch the lowest of the three. The question is the last three articulated pitches of the 1st violin in IV. Allegro vivace of Dvořák Symphony No.2 in B♭ major Op.4 and which of them is the lowest in pitch.

Round 0 majority already pointed to a tonic B♭-major close with a first-violin tonic arpeggio. The minority outliers were B♭–G–F tail with lowest F, and A–G–E / final E neighbour figures.

Round 1 public responses show strong convergence. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 now state explicitly the same reading: the coda is a normal V–I in B♭ major and the 1st violins are left with the broken tonic triad written descending in the violin register

f′ – d′ – b♭  = F – D – B♭

e.g. modern engraving F5–D5–B♭4, older / scientific reading F4–D4–B♭3. In pitch order F > D > B♭, so the last attack is the tonic B♭ and it is the lowest of the three distinct attacks. The B♭ is the root of the final B♭–D–F tutti on which the symphony is left.

Colleague 10 now retracts the earlier E upbeat reading and agrees the descending F–D–B♭ is the first-desk line, the E/A–G reading being a misreading/confusion with an inner voice/after-beat. Colleague 7 now says the B♭ reading matches the printed first-violin part and the A–G–E reading belongs to inner voices/different desks. Exact octave labeling remains edition-dependent but note name is unambiguously B♭.
